questions.answer: Yes. The last write handshake is Ec, the later of the AW and W transfers (or the shared edge). bvalid is 1 in the cycle that starts at Ec. Read data is valid in the cycle that starts at Ear. A low bready or rready does not delay this. It only keeps valid and the payload held until the B or R transfer.
An unmapped write changes no register and answers SLVERR. Word indices PARA_NUM_REGS to 15 (the gap below 0x40) are unmapped, as are all word indices 17 and above.
OKAY. A write to the status register changes nothing and answers 2'b00.

The spec defines it in full. A read address is held in cycle n if its AR transfer happened at an edge e <= n-1, its R transfer has not happened at any edge <= n-1, and i_rst_n has not been 0 since the AR transfer.

A reset at any time since the AW or W transfer ends the held state. No transfer can happen at an edge where i_rst_n is 0, so a B transfer cannot occur at a reset edge. The reset discards the held state and the response.
The elaboration error is only recommended ('should'). Behaviour with illegal parameters is unspecified and is not verified, so the error is not checked.
There is no overlap. 16 registers occupy 0x00 to 0x3C, and the status register is at 0x40 (word index 16).
Reset assertion is asynchronous. Release is synchronous to i_clk. Outputs therefore take their reset values on assertion without waiting for a clock edge.
Yes. o_regs is an output with reset value 0. REQ-RST-004 covers every output, so it includes o_regs. Flip-flops are reset asynchronously.

The held state is discarded and no register is written by it after release. A register changes only at Ec, when both address and data have been taken, so a transaction with only the address held has not changed any register.

The terms are defined. R1 is the first rising edge with i_rst_n at 1 after a reset period. Ec is the later of Ea and Ew. Eb, Ear and Er are the B, AR and R transfer edges. 'Held' runs from the transfer until the B (or R) transfer, with a reset also ending it. A held address or data is not held in the cycle after the B transfer, and awready and wready return to 1 in the cycle that starts at Eb.
Ec is the later of Ea and Ew, or the shared edge if both happen together. It is not the edge after. bvalid is 1 in the cycle that starts at Ec, and the register is written at Ec.
No conflict. awready and wready are 0 while the address or data is held. Held lasts until the B transfer. They return to 1 in the cycle that starts at Eb. They do not go high before the B handshake.

The spec covers all three orderings of Ear against Ec for the same register. Ear equal to Ec returns the old value. Ear after Ec returns the new value. Ear before Ec is unaffected by the write. o_regs shows the new value from the cycle that starts at Ec. The read returns the value in the cycle that ends at Ear, which is the old one.

No. While a response is pending, the address or data (or read address) is held, so the readies are 0. The readies do not depend on the valids; they depend only on the held state. The two rule sets are consistent.
i_status is sampled at Ear, the AR transfer edge. It is the value in the cycle that ends at Ear. It is then held until Er. Example 3 shows this.
The ranges are stated. PARA_NUM_REGS is 1 to 16. PARA_ADDR_W is 7 to 16, and 7 is the minimum that reaches the status register at 0x40.

Yes. Every write transaction has bvalid from Ec, with the normal write timing. A write with wstrb = 0 answers exactly like a strobed write to the same address and changes no register. A status write answers OKAY and changes nothing.
Yes. Bits [1:0] have no effect and are not an error. The decode uses the word index, so an unaligned address in the unmapped range is still unmapped and answers SLVERR.

They are quoted in the spec. RST-004: on assertion every output takes its reset value without waiting for a clock edge. RST-005: no transfer at an edge where i_rst_n is 0. RST-009: a reset discards held write address, write data, write response and read address, with no response and no write after release.

Yes. With 8 registers 0x20 to 0x3C is unmapped, and 0x44 up to the top of the bus is also unmapped. CFG-BASE highlights the 0x20 to 0x3C gap. Addresses above 0x3C are covered by the register map and by the required unmapped-address scenarios.

With 16 registers, REG_0 to REG_15 are at 0x00 to 0x3C, and 0x40 is the status register. 'No unmapped address below 0x44' means 0x00 to 0x3C are registers and 0x40 is the status register. There is no conflict.

No check applies before the first reset assertion, and REQ-VER-010 is included in that. Reset is driven from time zero for at least 2 cycles, so checking is from reset on. 'Every cycle' in REQ-VER-010 applies after that point.
No conflict. Assertion is asynchronous, so REQ-VER-021 asserts reset between clock edges. Release must be synchronous, so the testbench changes i_rst_n away from clock edges, which fits both.

Yes, they are consistent. Inputs must be defined (no X or Z) while i_rst_n is 1. During reset the valids may be 0 or 1. A reset ends the stability obligation, so after R1 the manager may drop a valid or change a payload. A valid at 1 after R1 is a new request.

The behaviour is consistent. The readies are 0 during reset and in the cycle that ends at R1, and are 1 from R1. A reset mid-transaction ends every held state, so the R1 rule applies after it. D-010 covers the normal return after a B or R transfer. R1 is the first rising edge with i_rst_n at 1 after reset.

bresp, rresp and rdata are 0 only while i_rst_n is 0. After release and before a response, their values are unspecified and not checked. The checker compares them only when the valid is 1 or i_rst_n is 0. Before the first reset assertion, nothing is checked.
